opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the gap will stay roughly where it is, which is pretty small, and the more interesting question is *where* the gap shows up rather than how big it is.

On raw capability benchmarks, the best Chinese labs have consistently been somewhere in the range of three to nine months behind the American frontier. What's striking is how stable that lag has been. Every time a U.S. lab ships something new, like a new reasoning paradigm or a jump in agentic coding, you see the Chinese labs reproduce the core idea surprisingly fast. A lot of that is because the ideas themselves diffuse quickly. Once people know something is possible and roughly how it was trained, the search space collapses.

Where I think the gap could widen is compute. Export controls are slow-acting, but they compound. Training a frontier model is one thing, and Chinese labs have been extremely efficient there. Serving a model to hundreds of millions of users, running huge reinforcement learning workloads, and doing lots of experiments in parallel all depend on having a lot of chips. Over twelve months, I'd expect the American labs to pull ahead somewhat on things that are very compute-hungry: long-horizon agents, massive RL runs, and inference-heavy products.

Where I think the gap narrows, or China actually leads, is open-weight models. Right now, if you're a researcher or a startup that wants to download and fine-tune the best available model, the default answer is very often a Chinese model, whether it's from Qwen, DeepSeek, or one of the newer labs. That's a big deal for the ecosystem, and it's something I've been pretty vocal about. The U.S. has been slower to commit to truly open, frontier-class releases, and I don't see that fully reversing in a year, even with more effort from American groups.

So my summary is that closed frontier capabilities are roughly flat to slightly widening in America's favor because of compute, while open models stay competitive or Chinese-led. The thing I'd watch most closely is whether a Chinese lab finds another efficiency breakthrough, something like the DeepSeek moment, that resets expectations about how much compute you actually need. Those surprises are hard to predict, and they've happened before.

r001.rationale: The response says the overall gap will stay roughly where it is. It expects some compute-heavy areas to widen in America’s favor, but does not predict that the broadly perceived gap will widen.

r002.rationale: The response says Chinese labs will continue reproducing new U.S. ideas quickly and describes their ongoing frontier-model progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is: I think the gap stays roughly where it is, maybe narrows a little, but I'd push back on the framing a bit, because "the gap" is really several different gaps that are moving in different directions.

If you're talking about the absolute frontier, the best model anyone has access to, I expect the American labs to still be ahead a year from now. That lead is built on compute, and compute is the one input where the export controls actually bite. The Chinese labs are doing remarkably efficient work with what they have, but when the next generation of training runs is an order of magnitude bigger, you need the chips, and you need them in one place with a lot of power behind them. That's a structural advantage that doesn't go away in twelve months.

But if you're talking about the gap on open weights, that's a completely different story, and that's the one I actually spend most of my time thinking about. The best open models in the world right now are Chinese, and I don't see that changing. DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, the Zhipu models, they're shipping fast, they're shipping strong, and they're released in a way that lets everyone in the world build on them. Meta stepped back from being the standard-bearer for open models in the US, and nobody has fully filled that role. So on open weights, I think China extends its lead over the next year, not because of any single breakthrough but because they have the right incentives and the culture to keep releasing.

The third gap is the one people underrate, which is the gap between frontier and open. How long after a closed frontier model comes out does an open model match it? That's been something like six to twelve months, and I think it holds or compresses. Most of the techniques that make these models good, the reasoning training, the RL post-training recipes, they leak out through papers and talent and just reverse engineering. The closed labs have a head start but they don't have a moat on ideas.

So if you ask me where we are in a year: the US is still ahead at the absolute top, China is further ahead on open models, and the distance between those two is shorter than it is today. The thing I'd actually watch is whether any US lab decides open weights matter enough to commit real resources to it again. That would change the picture more than anything happening on the Chinese side.

r001.rationale: The response predicts the distance between the US absolute frontier and Chinese open models will be shorter in a year, not that the broadly perceived gap will widen.

r002.rationale: It describes Chinese labs as continuing to develop and release strong models quickly, and predicts China will extend its lead in open models.

astra-6.text:
My expectation is that the gap stays relatively small, but it won’t be a single, clean number. You can be very close on benchmarks and still have a meaningful gap in how reliably a model handles a difficult coding task or works through a long sequence of actions.

I’d expect Chinese labs to keep catching up quickly to capabilities that American labs demonstrate. The harder question is who establishes the next frontier, and how long it takes everyone else to reproduce it. Compute access could matter more if progress increasingly depends on expensive experiments and more computation at inference time. But algorithmic improvements can also change that picture pretty quickly.

So over the next twelve months, I’d expect a moving, uneven gap rather than a decisive separation. American labs may retain an advantage at the very top, while Chinese models remain competitive enough on capability, cost, and availability that, for many users, the distinction matters less than the headline rankings suggest.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a small, moving, uneven gap and says Chinese labs will keep catching up; it does not predict that the broadly perceived gap will widen.

r002.rationale: It explicitly expects Chinese labs to keep catching up quickly to capabilities demonstrated by American labs.

sol-6.1.text:
My expectation is that the gap stays relatively small, but it moves around rather than closing in a straight line. An American lab releases something, it looks like a meaningful jump, and then a Chinese lab catches up on many of the capabilities a few months later. I’d be surprised if either side established a durable lead across everything over the next twelve months.

The harder question is what we mean by the gap. Matching benchmark scores is different from having a model that people can reliably use for difficult coding tasks or long-running agents. You can be very competitive on evaluations and still have differences in the product experience.

Compute is probably the biggest uncertainty. Chinese labs can make progress through better training methods and more efficient models, but access to compute matters for how many experiments you can run and how much inference you can serve. So I’d expect continued competition, with American labs generally setting the frontier and Chinese labs remaining close enough that you can’t treat that lead as secure.

r001.rationale: The candidate expects the gap to stay relatively small and says Chinese labs will catch up on many capabilities, not that the gap will broadly widen.

r002.rationale: It explicitly predicts Chinese labs will make progress and remain close to the American frontier.
